name: Kéo
catalog_citation: Baird, Louise. 2002. A grammar of Kéo: an Austronesian language of East Nusantara. PhD thesis, Australian National University (hdl 1885/9446).
catalog_locator: sec. 2.6 Stress, p.53 (PDF p.49 of the ANU bitstream 'Baird Thesis ')
catalog_quote: 2.6 Stress. Stress in Indonesian languages is often a controversial issue. However, it is possible to make generalisations. Stress in Kéo is predictable: it typically falls on the penultimate syllable of the word. The exception to this is in disyllabic words in which there is a schwa in the first syllable, in which case stress falls on the ultimate syllable. Primary stress in compounds, as in simple words, falls on the penultimate syllable. Stress in Indonesian loan words also falls on the penultimate syllable. Kéo has one proclitic, the numeral one ~ ha (see §6.4 and §9.2.2). Stress remains on the penultimate syllable in disyllabic words which have the clitic attached to them. The clitic itself is typically unstressed, and is often realised as a schwa.

audit.reasoning: The classification rests on the sole reference grammar of the language (Baird 2002 ANU thesis), which we hold as the ANU scan; the deciding passage (sec. 2.6, p.53) is confirmed verbatim on the rendered page image, and the supporting phonotactics pages (2.4-2.5, pp.50-52: all syllables open (C)V, simple words 1-2 syllables, schwa in the vowel inventory) are also held and match the record's 'heavy'/'wcls' notes. Glottolog's bibliography has no competing grammar, phonology or sketch; Elias 2018 (the only other phonology-tagged work covering Kéo, fetched sources now from Leiden, open access) takes its Kéo data from Baird and says nothing about Kéo stress. No database contradictions are recorded. Only nit: the domain-quote locator should read p.51, not p.52. engine scraping blocked), so the sweep for Indonesian-language skrip

sources.quote: No statement on Kéo stress. Stress is described only for Lio ('Stress has a low functional load in Lio and is usually initial in isolated words'; schwa words variable). Kéo (Udiworowatu dialect) enters only the comparative reconstruction, with data from Baird 2002.
